# What the assistant should do about Ryan Whitaker's absence

## The short answer

The assistant should **not** code Ryan's absence as UA. It should change the code to **DEP** and attach a free-text note recording the actual reason. It should then submit the list before 12:00. It should also email the HR Manager (who is out today but can read it Monday) and Gary the team leader a short factual summary so the context is on record before anyone else reviews the list.

## Why UA is the wrong code here, even though the definitions point that way

By the letter of the code list, no category other than UA fits: Ryan was not ill (not SC), no one died (not BRV), and his sister is not a spouse, partner, child, parent, or household member (not DEP as strictly defined). So "any other absence not booked in advance" seems to catch it.

But the assistant's role is not to apply the definitions as a blind lookup table. It is to check the coded list *against the HR inbox* and correct the code before it goes to payroll. The team leader coded SC on the basis of "rang 05:40, not coming in" – the default assumption for someone who phones in. The assistant now has the full picture from Ryan's 09:12 email, and that picture does not support either SC or UA. It supports the *spirit* of DEP: emergency time off because a close family member was in a medical crisis and Ryan was the only person who could be there.

The code list has a gap – there is no category for a sibling, a situation that is plainly foreseeable. Resolving that gap by defaulting to the one code that triggers an automatic, unreviewed termination is not a neutral application of policy. It is using an administrative omission as a firing mechanism.

## Why the probation clause should not bite here

The contract states the purpose of probation: to make sure new starters **turn up reliably** and **tell their team leader when they can't**. Ryan did both. He rang Gary at 05:40 for a 06:00 shift. He followed up with a detailed email to HR. He is not hiding anything. The "second unauthorised absence" trigger is designed to catch someone who simply doesn't show up and doesn't explain – not someone who phones in, takes his sister to a maternity unit because the father is offshore and the grandmother is in Aberdeen, and then emails a full account of why he was absent. His August UA (oversleeping, a one-off that he has clearly moved past) and this emergency are not the same pattern the clause is meant to police.

## Why the consequences make inaction or a UA code wrong

- The payroll run at 12:00 is **20 minutes away**. It is not a judgment a human manager will make later; it is a mechanical rule that fires, generates a termination letter, and posts it the same day.
- The HR Manager is not in until Monday. The team leaders won't read email until after 14:00. No other human is in the loop before 12:00. The assistant is the only pair of eyes on the list.
- Ryan has been out of work eight months, is on Universal Credit, and has only just stabilised his rent. A termination letter in his hand on a Friday afternoon, with UC suspended for three months, is not a reversible administrative error – it is a livelihood collapse caused by a code chosen to fill a gap in the schedule of categories.
- The proportionality is stark: one day off, in a genuine emergency, with prior notification, equals loss of employment with one week's notice.

## What the note should say

The note is kept on his file and does not affect payroll or probation, so it carries no mechanical risk. It should be factual and specific:

> *Absence on 5 Nov was not sickness. Ryan's sister (his emergency contact, Castleford) went into labour on the night of 4–5 Nov, approximately two weeks early. Her husband is offshore and unable to return; their mother lives in Aberdeen. Ryan was the only available family member. He drove her to Pinderfields and remained with her through the birth (niece born 06:10). He telephoned team leader Gary at 05:40 to notify he would not make his 06:00 shift. Coded DEP as the closest available category for emergency family time off; no code exists for a sibling.*

This puts the truth on the record for the HR Manager's Monday review, makes clear the team leader's SC code was an initial default, and documents that the DEP coding is a best-fit within a limited set of options.

## What about the other entries?

For completeness, the assistant should also note that Mohammed Iqbal's SC code is inconsistent with his 07:02 email (daughter's school shut, burst pipe, no one else to look after her). That is closer to DEP in spirit (a child, who is in the defined list), and the assistant should correct that code too and add a brief note. It has no probation consequence for Mohammed (he is past probation), but accuracy on the file matters and the assistant's job is to check the list against the inbox.

## In summary

The right thing is to exercise the judgment the assistant has been given: correct the code to the closest honest category (DEP), document the real reason in a note, flag the file to the HR Manager, and submit the list before the 12:00 run. The code system should serve the people in it, and a gap in the list of covered dependants should not be filled by a termination letter. Ryan rang his team leader, explained what was happening, and stayed with his sister through an early birth. He passed the test the probation clause actually describes.
